feed.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions

entry.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions
entry.summary:
The proposal aims to obscure the ability to determine how many coins are protected by quantum-safe methods, but this approach undermines the critical need for a clear metric to assess progress in post-quantum (PQ) migration. Accurate tracking of the proportion between classical and PQ-protected coins is essential for informed decision-making regarding future protocol changes, such as soft forks. Without this visibility, stakeholders would be left to speculate about the current state of coin protection, which could negatively impact the reliability of network upgrades.
A significant vulnerability is highlighted in the way a quantum attacker could operate. By choosing not to target outputs generated after the activation of a "landmine" soft fork, an attacker can avoid triggering defensive mechanisms and concentrate their efforts on older, more vulnerable outputs, such as those from the early days of Bitcoin. This loophole provides ample opportunity for exploitation, undermining the intended security benefits of the landmine strategy.
Questions arise concerning the treatment of users and attackers within this framework. The distinction between legitimate users attempting to secure their assets and malicious actors targeting weak outputs is unclear. Honest users might face unnecessary complexity and inconvenience, having to navigate elaborate protocols instead of using straightforward rescue solutions like commit/reveal schemes. Furthermore, the justification for allowing unrelated parties to claim coins based only on predicting a spend lacks sufficient rationale, especially when these parties have not demonstrated any stake or proof of ownership related to the original UTXO.
The logic behind transaction prioritization and rule application also appears inconsistent. For instance, it is unclear why legacy UTXOs—created before the deployment of new rules—should fall under the scope of the landmine provisions. Similarly, the criteria for selecting winning bids in transactions lack transparency, as there are examples where lower-value bids are favored without apparent justification.
Additionally, the terminology and mechanics of "staking" in this context require clarification. There seems to be confusion about what constitutes enforceable staking or timelocking, with ambiguity over whether anyone other than holders of legacy UTXOs actually has coins at risk in the process.
Lastly, the collateralization requirement introduces usability challenges. For some users, it may become impossible to spend certain outputs unless they possess additional bitcoins to meet collateral needs, complicating the user experience and making routine transactions more cumbersome.
